utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those following our proceedings. Before we start or continue with the witness, I would kindly ask the Prosecutor in relation to the next witness, what the reasons may be to request two and a half hours of cross-examination. You will recall that it was the practice during the Prosecution case that Mr. Tolimir always requested, or most cases, requested the same time for cross-examination as the Prosecution requested for the examination-in-chief of their own witnesses. Are there specific reasons to extend this time for cross-examination of the witness? Mr. Tolimir had requested one hour and a half for his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Mr. President, I think I can be of some assistance to the Trial Chamber. One of the reasons why the amount of time has been requested with respect to the next witness by the Prosecution is in excess of the amount of time that Mr. Tolimir intends to examine him is because the nature of this witness's testimony, as I understand it, potentially bears on the question of alibi which relates to General Tolimir's whereabouts following the end of July. His ability to communicate with the Main Staff and other elements of the VRS -- other VRS units, as well as his physical location is at issue. The 65 ter summary does not -- is not particularly extensive in terms of the information it provides concerning those issues, and in order to allow us the ability to cross-examine this witness on those issues as they may arise during the course of his direct testimony, we've made an allowance for that, and that's the reason why we've asked for more time than we normally would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, what is the position of the Defence in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May the Lord bring peace upon this house, and may this trial be concluded according to providence and God's will, not according to my wishes. The Defence takes the position that the Prosecution may do whatever they want to do, that they are at liberty to prove whatever they want to prove, and finally, that they can extend the time required for examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The Chamber will consider the situation and come back to it before the -- or at the beginning of the testimony of that witness. The current witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Skrbic. Welcome back. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies today. Before Mr. Vanderpuye gets the floor, I have one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: During the course of your testimony, you testified about the way you have collected your information, about the kind of documents you have received in order to prepare your expertise and your expert report. I would kindly ask you to explain, in general, the method you followed in preparing the two reports you have provided to the Defence, and the Defence to the Chamber. What were the principles of your work, how did you collect your information, and especially did you seek guidance from anybody how to prepare such an expert -- since you told us it's the first time that you are as an expert testifying in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have received a lot of documents, as I already said. Then I made a kind of preliminary review of the documents by opening each folder and each file, and for all those documents that at first glance this -- I decided that they cannot be of any use for preparing my expert report according to my idea and according to my proposition of how it should look like, I did not mark such documents. Now, as for the documents I believe that can be of use in the course of preparing my expert report, I marked them in an appropriate manner and that's how I finalised this preliminary inspection of the documents. Then I went back to the ones that I marked and I read them more thoroughly and marked, in a way that the current information technology allows me to do, such sections that I copied into a new folder which I entitled: "Working Material." Thereby I created a working material basis from a large number of documents. On the basis of that file, I started preparing my expert report. Of course, I did not include all the parts of the documents that I copied in this working material folder because, quite simply, I didn't have enough space or time to provide such a voluminous report. This, Mr. President, is the way how I approached the preparation of my expert report. I did not consult anyone with regard to any single document or any other issue relating to my expert report for that matter. Everything I did I did independently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your answer triggered two follow-up questions. You said: "I have received a lot of documents ..." Can you tell us from whom did you receive these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I received the documents from the -- General Miletic's Defence team and General Tolimir's Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When did this process of providing you with documents start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This process commenced at the moment when I was approved by the Tribunal's Registry to become a member of General Miletic's team as an investigator, and it ended by the submission of documents from General Tolimir's team prior to the preparation of this report of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your involvement in the two cases were of a different quality. In the Miletic case, you were an investigator for the Defence team; here, you are testifying as an expert witness. Can you tell me when this process of providing you with document from the Defence in this current case started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, the process of the provision of documents started after the receipt of a decision that my nomination as a military expert has been approved by the Registry, and after that the Defence team of General Tolimir started sending me documents, and I think that was when the decision was taken. That was in the 2nd of May of last year --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The second half of May, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us at the beginning of your testimony that you took part in a conference in Moscow and that you published, after that, a paper on this same topic as we are dealing with. On which documents did you rely at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I relied on the documents that I had received from General Miletic's Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I forgot when this conference in Moscow took place. Can you repeat the time, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was in April 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question. You said in your first answer: "I decided that they," referring to documents, "cannot be of any use for preparing my expert report according to my idea and according to my proposition of how it should look like." What was your idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My idea was - and I really apologise to you for having to repeat this once again - to follow the fate of the Muslim survivors and thereby establish whether there are any differences in the period before and after the VRS action. All the documents that could not fit or serve the application of such methodology I discarded, such as, for example, photographs because I didn't need them in order to verify the facts and were not able to provide me with any specific evidence that would help me to check the actual number of potentially missing number of Muslims as compared to the number that existed before the VRS operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said -- the question was for you whether there are any differences in the period before and after the VRS action in relation to the fate of the Muslim survivors. Could you explain what your proposition was in that respect? You said you had a certain proposition how your expert report should look like. What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My thesis was that this methodology that I had chosen and the method of conducting research that I adhered to can, in a very convincing manner, demonstrate whether there were fewer inhabitants of Srebrenica in the aftermath of Krivaja 95 operation as opposed to the number that existed in Srebrenica before the operation. So my proposition was that this is a proper method that would help me to prove whether there were such enormous numbers of victims or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I read your reports carefully. There is one thing missing, in my view. I didn't see any list of publications or documents you have taken into account while drafting your report. This is quite unusual.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report, wherever I made reference to any number, I put the reference number of the documents that I was relying upon, and in the event of using tables or charts about the population, then under each of such graphics I provided an explanation about the sources from which these specific number of inhabitants were taken. So I didn't include footnotes or endnotes in a standard manner but, instead, quite simply, whenever I used a number taken from any document, I would insert in brackets the number of the document that I used as an outsourcing tool or made a reference to it in some other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, I saw it in your text. Thank you for providing me with your answers. Mr. Vanderpuye, I took some time before you get the floor. You have it now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, once again. Good afternoon to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something that's emerged from the discussion you just had now with the Presiding Judge, and it is that your report -- or, rather, you prepared two reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One is the population analysis and the other one is the military report, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so with respect to the answers that you gave the Presiding Judge concerning the documents that you relied on or didn't rely on, did that relate to one report or the other or to both?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To both.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the objective of your reports, were they the same for both?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They cannot have one common objective, these two reports, because in my first report I wanted to check, as I said, whether it is correct that over 7.000 able-bodied men had been executed. The second report was intended to take into account all military events, whether they be combat events or those relating to military operations, and to put them in the context of a mutual conflict so that the Trial Chamber and everyone else who is interested in that can perceive these events in the context of the conflict instead of perceiving it only in a one-sided manner, as if only one army existed and the other army did not exist at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could have D368 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You'll recognise this as your report on the movement of the Srebrenica population, yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to page 27 in the English and page 30 in the Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for you, sir, I'd like to focus you on the paragraph that starts after the reference to P1268. It's just after the redacted portions end in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For our purposes, it's in the same position, roughly, on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There you write that: [As read] "None of your attempts to establish whether there were large-scale Muslim casualties during and after the fighting for Srebrenica have been successful. One thing is beyond doubt: That you have made efforts to find any sort of data which might perhaps point to their being large-scale Muslim casualties during and after that fighting. Those efforts have obviously been in vain, for even hypothetical situations which are indubitably directed towards proving that there were large-scale Muslim casualties with the numbers killed during the breakout being deliberately excluded from the equation have not borne any fruit because we have reliably determined that at least 3.000 (5.000) BiH Army soldiers left the enclave and joined that army's 2nd Corps and were not registered as refugees." Then you say: "The number of 897 possible Muslim victims cannot, therefore, be regarded as reliable and cannot be used as possible evidence or fact regarding large-scale Muslim casualties." With respect to your efforts to find any sort of data which might, perhaps, point to there being large-scale Muslim casualties, it is true that you disregarded forensic evidence that was available to you, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only partially correct. Sir, I explained to you that I am not a forensic expert and I know next to nothing about forensic science. When you showed me Mr. Brunborg's document on Thursday, dated 2009, bearing the -- citing the number of 7.000 something, I told you that by casting a cursory glance at any document - and that was the first time I saw the document - after I briefly looked at it, I wasn't able to establish which period is covered in the document with regard to the casualties, whether it is covering the whole period of the conflict or just July and August 1995. That was the reason why I partly discarded or partly decided not to use some of the forensic -- forensic reports, because I don't want to swim in a deep water if I am not a good swimmer. Let me tell you one more thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I am going to ask you to answer my question. My question was whether or not you disregarded that evidence. You can answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. And I couldn't use it anyway because, as I told you, that was the first time that I saw that document here last Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You didn't ask General Tolimir for that document or documents like it in preparing your report, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, how could I have known about the existence of those documents if nobody gave them to me? As for those that were given to me and concerned forensic science, I studied them and I have just told you why I didn't take that information and that data into account when I did my calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So tell us what you mean in your report where you say that you made efforts to find any sort of data which might, perhaps, point to there being large-scale Muslim casualties during and after the fighting. What any sort of data do you have in mind in this particular passage that's now before us?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information concerning the number of the population before and after the operation launched by the Army of Republika Srpska, that's the information that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Isn't the whole purpose of determining what the population was before and after the crime to determine the possibility that people were killed in the manner that's described in this indictment, by the thousands in mass summary executions? Wasn't that the whole point of it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The point and the purpose was -- and I really apologise. You are forcing me to repeat one and the same thing over and over again. It was always the point for me to check if people were missing, and if they indeed were missing, how many went missing after the operation in comparison with the number of the population of Srebrenica before the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, doesn't the number of missing and dead people that I showed you the other day contained in Mr. -- Dr. Brunborg and Dr. Tabeau's report bear on the question of how many missing and dead people there were after the conflict, after Srebrenica collapsed? Doesn't it bear directly on the issue that you were studying?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are just asking me does not fit within my research methodology; therefore, I am in no position to give a different answer. At the same time, I don't want to go over the same grounds again. I don't want to discuss my research methodology again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you are here to explain your research methodology as often as necessary. This is your obligation. And this sentence put to you from your report doesn't relate to missing persons but to Muslim casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the sentence that has been shown to me and that, indeed, is a product of my own work, I can see that this sentence refers to the possible number of those Muslims who went missing after the VRS operation. It doesn't apply to anything else. When I said in this courtroom that even hypothetical situations did not yield the result of 7.000 or even more inhabitants of Srebrenica missing after the operation, this means that I had studied such a hypothetical situation, that I did my calculations for such a hypothetical situation and made my inferences based on that, and you will find that hypothetical situation in my report. One is just a hypothesis, another is an extreme hypothesis, and there is a third one which is also another extreme hypothesis. I really wanted to check whether 7.000 and more militarily able-bodied men or inhabitants of Srebrenica, indeed, went missing after the operation in Srebrenica in comparison with the situation as it was before that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your statement in your report that you made efforts to find any sort of data pointing to these mass casualties is untrue, isn't it, Mr. Skrbic? You didn't make efforts to find any sort of data reporting to -- relating to the mass casualties as alleged in this case. You used some data that suited the ends to which you sought to achieve, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I used facts, and I found those facts in documents. I didn't deal with anything else. The only thing I dealt with were facts. If it says in the documents that have been displayed here that in Srebrenica, before the VRS operation there were 40.000 inhabitants, or 38.000 according to some sources, or 42.000 according to yet other sources, and I did my calculations based on the figure of 38.000, as well as on the figure of 40, as well as on the figure of 42.000, what objections can you make to that? How can you wrong that [as interpreted]? I was very consistent. I didn't want -- I didn't have the intention to make my calculations based on median values. I made my calculations respecting the principle of consistency in science. Using the lower part of the range as well as the upper part of the range, and I just let the results show what they did, and they showed exactly what I stated in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I am just trying to get to the bottom of your reference here that you used or made efforts to find any sort of data. You haven't been able to answer that so far. Let me ask you about what precedes that immediately, and we can see just a glimpse of it on the top of the screen here of your reference to certain statements. You made reference to certain statements in your report, correct? Of witnesses, survivors, those types of people.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you relied on those statements in order to determine your objectives, which was to find out how many people were missing as a result or following the collapse of Srebrenica by comparing how many people you found and registered against how many people were in the census or the population studies before the fall of Srebrenica. Right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I relied on the information provided by the witnesses whom I mentioned in my expert report. And now I am going to tell you something that will disappoint you, just as I was disappointed with the fact that I am going to share with you. Whenever I did my calculations and whenever I used information about the number of soldiers of the 28th Division who managed to break through - and their Commander-in-Chief, General Rasim Delic, said that 5.000 had broken through, mostly unscathed - in every example of my calculations, whenever I used that figure, I would end up with results that were really surprising, even for me. Every time I ended up with a number of able-bodied men after the operation which was higher than the number of them who were found in Srebrenica prior to the VRS operation. And this is just not logical and natural. However, facts are facts. I could not avoid that. An old Latin maxim says: "Contra factum non datur argumentum," which means you cannot argue facts. There is no proof against facts. And let me tell you one more thing. In my calculations I did not use the number of 3.000 soldiers of the 28th Division who were killed or died during the breakthrough. Why is that? Why didn't I use that number? I didn't use that number, sir, because every calculation based on the 3.000 soldiers who died during the breakthrough would also demonstrate that the number of able-bodied men was higher after the VRS operation in comparison with the number of able-bodied men prior to the operation. I didn't use that number because I really felt embarrassed because I knew that that was not natural. The facts that I used are simply facts. I didn't make them up. They are facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The numbers you came up with didn't take account of the prisoners that were in VRS custody following the fall of Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can answer that yes or no, Mr. Skrbic. You either did or you didn't.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You didn't take consideration of the testimony evidence that was provided by VRS members in this case concerning the custody of those prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deliberately didn't use any Serb sources or any other source that might be perceived as being close to us Serbian sources, and I did that because I wanted to avoid any objection or accusation that I used wrong information. I only -- the only sources I used were BiH Army units and international organisations and those forces that were deployed in Srebrenica during the relevant period and that carried out certain tasks over there based on UN mandate or without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who Drazen Erdemovic is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the media. And in several documents I came across his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You know that he was a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that in documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You know that that detachment was controlled by the intelligence administration of the Main Staff of the VRS at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There is no single unit in any army, which includes the VRS, or any other state, that is under control or directly subordinated to any other organ but the organ that is authorised to be in command and issue tasks. The 10th Sabotage Unit, or whatever you wish to call it, or any other unit, certainly could not have been subordinated to the intelligence and security sector or any other administration or sector during the relevant period of time. That's how things are in a military. This is the principle of army organisation. If things were different, the main principle on which every military rests would be disturbed, and that principle is the singleness and unity of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who Colonel Petar Salapura is or was in July 1995, his position in the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know from documents. I know that he was chief of the security administration of the intelligence and security sector of the General Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We may have a translation issue. Could you repeat your answer, please, a little slowly.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Colonel Petar Salapura was, during the relevant period of time, in July and August 1995, chief of the security -- intelligence administration of the sector for intelligence and security in the General Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Salapura in that position give orders to the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in the military, orders and tasks are issued only by authorised officers. The only authorised officer to issue orders to subordinated units is the commander or a person authorised by him. In the absence of a commander in the VRS, this could have been done by his deputy, and during that period of time that was the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware that Colonel Salapura gave orders to the 10th Sabotage Detachment in 1995? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he gave orders. If he did, I don't know whether he was authorised to do so. I have just explained the functioning of a military and the principle of the singleness and unity of command. I told you who has the authority to issue orders to subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who Dragomir Pecanac is or was in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who Dragomir Pecanac is, but I don't know what he did in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know that he was a member of the intelligence administration at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've just told you I don't know what his position was in 1995, neither do I know what he did before or after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know that he testified that the 10th Sabotage Detachment in July 1995 was under the direct control of the intelligence administration in this case, transcript page 18133, lines 20 through 25, and transcript page 18134, lines 10 through 12. Do you know that, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't know what any of the witnesses in this case testified about. As far as I see things, perhaps I should know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you didn't take into consideration in drafting your report on the population of Srebrenica concerning the victims of the crimes perpetrated after its fall the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You know that his unit of the 10th Sabotage Detachment took part in the execution of what he described as over a thousand to 1200 Muslim prisoners at the Branjevo military farm on the 16th of July? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that in the indictment that you drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He also provided evidence that there were another 500 people that were in the Pilica cultural centre about whom he was approached to go and kill. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I have a feeling that the interpreter made quite long breaks in the question, so I was not in a position to understand your question fully, so could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware that Drazen Erdemovic testified that after the killings at the Branjevo farm, he was approached about killing another group of prisoners, about 500 of them, at the Pilica cultural centre or the Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he testified, and I've just told you that I did not take into account that information provided either by him or by anybody else. I didn't take any of that information into account when I did my calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I'll give it to you now. You've just heard me mention 1.000 to 1200 and now 500. How would that affect your calculations? Would it make it so that the population following the fall of Srebrenica exceeded the population before its fall, according to your calculations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to do another calculation in order to be able to answer your question. I can't tell you off the top of my head. I need time to do my calculations. I need to compare the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You didn't take into consideration the testimony of Momir Nikolic who testified that on 12 July, he was told by the chief of security of the Drina Corps that: "All the balijas were going to be killed"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I never used Momir Nikolic's testimony. I am not even sure that I read it with any deal of attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He also testified that the chief of security in the Main Staff in the sector of security and intelligence, Ljubisa Beara, told him that the prisoners in Bratunac were to be transferred to Zvornik where they were to be killed, and that he transmitted that order to the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade, Drago Nikolic. And he told him about that order on the evening of 13 July 1995. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who Tanacko Tanic is or was in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name? I heard Talic, but can you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tanacko Tanic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The name doesn't ring a bell. I never heard the name before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In July 1995 he was a member of the command of the Zvornik Brigade who testified in this trial about what he saw when he went to the Orahovac school on the afternoon of 14 July 1995. In part, he testified that he saw Drago Nikolic at the school, Vujadin Popovic at the school, both security officers within the security organ of the VRS. He testified that he saw a number of prisoners in the schools and that he was there until he saw a group of prisoners being loaded onto a truck to be transported, obviously, to the execution site and heard gun-shots that evening when he left the area from that direction. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have told you that the name doesn't ring a bell, how could I be in a position to know what that person said or testified or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You might have heard about prisoners being killed at the Orahovac school or nearby. Did you hear about that? That is, in the context of writing your report or before you wrote your report.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the number of those who were executed or detained and transferred to the Zvornik Brigade and then executed, I heard all that from the -- or learned about all that from the indictment in this case. As far as I can remember, in the first part of my report I did not leave out any of those figures, and I took them into account when I did my calculations. I will not repeat what kind of result I ended up with because that would just be taxing on both you and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you heard the name Lazar Ristic before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. The name doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander of the 4th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade who also testified in this trial. He was requested to supply ten men to the school and was told, later, that those ten men had been approached about forming an execution squad to kill the prisoners at that school. When I say "kill," I mean summarily execute them. Did you hear that evidence, perhaps, someplace else?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard about that testimony. I've just told you that that man's name doesn't even ring a bell. I've never heard that name before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, a moment ago you said facts are facts. This Trial Chamber has heard the evidence or received the evidence of numerous witnesses that attest to the fact that thousands upon thousands of prisoners in the custody of VRS units following the collapse of Srebrenica were summarily executed at several sites, in Zvornik and elsewhere, that their bodies were put in pits dug out by excavator operators who testified in this case about what pits they dug out, when they dug them out, and where. Are you telling this Trial Chamber that you have not reviewed any of the evidence as it relates to the disposition of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not read these testimonies. I read your indictment. I took over from it the information you provided with relation to the number of the people executed, captured, or transferred, and I used them in my calculations in the manner I already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You testified, I think it was on Thursday, that you skipped over some photographs, yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And I repeated that this morning in my response to the Trial Chamber President, stating that these kind of documents did not serve my purpose and did not serve the objective that I set and that is why I didn't use them. And I'm telling you the same thing now, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P94.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have that in e-court, please. And we'll need to go to page 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I am showing you is an aerial image of the Nova Kasaba football stadium. As you can see from this particular exhibit, this is from 13 July at 1400 hours. You may recall that this is the same time as the exhibit I showed you earlier from Colonel Milomir Savcic, which talks about a thousand prisoners in Dusanova Kasaba. Do you remember that document that I showed you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you page 46 of this exhibit. This is an aerial image, as you can see from this exhibit, taken 13 July 1995, again at 1400 hours. This is at Sandici which, of course, you know is a different location than Novo Kasaba. And you can see in the centre of the picture or just below the centre of the picture a group of people. Do you see them there, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please assist me and point me to this group of people?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can blow that up. It's just below the centre of the picture, a little bit to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does that assist you, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really doing my best to discern that these are human beings, but no matter how hard I try, I really cannot say that these are people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall the document I showed you that was authored by Ljubisa Borovcanin, dated 13 July, the one that talked about 1500 prisoners and their numbers are growing by the hour? Do you remember that from Thursday?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P -- page, rather, 249 of this exhibit. Have you seen this photograph before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing this photograph before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the Branjevo farm execution. Let me show you page 250. Have you seen this photo before, Mr. Skrbic? These are the people that were found at the bottom of that grave, some of them.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you page 261 of this exhibit. These are a series of secondary graves along the Cancari road from one through twelve. Have you seen this or these photographs before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. And for each photograph that you are going to ask me in the future about, I said that whilst I was reviewing documents, whenever I came across a photograph, I decided that they were not useful for my calculations and therefore I did not utilise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you page 264. This is a photograph of the exhumation of Cancari 12. Have you seen this photograph before, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you page 196 of this exhibit. What we are looking at now is aerial imagery taken of the Kozluk execution site. On the left-hand of the screen you can see what the site looked like on 5 July 1995, and then you can see what the site looked like on 17 July 1995. And you can see a clear difference between those two photographs. Have you seen this or these images before, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. And now I can tell you this: Thank you for showing me this particular photograph so that I can finally give you any kind of answer relating to the pictures shown to me. A photograph is a frozen shot, and I cannot recognise, I cannot assert, I cannot give you any answer whether that was the actual situation or not. I wasn't there on the spot. I cannot tell you whether it was like this at the time or not. Now, in view of all the surveillance equipment available at the time, it is only natural -- it would have been natural for you to show us dynamic images and then there nobody should and would have any doubts about it. But as General Smith said in his evidence, he said that photographs were a good tool but they didn't show what was going on under the surface of the ground because photographs, as I said, are frozen images; therefore, I cannot give you a proper answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who Srecko Acimovic is or was in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. It was his unit that was associated with the prisoners that were brought to the Rocevic school and executed at this site here that I am showing you. Now, I take it you haven't read his testimony.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't, and I said that I didn't use any of the Serbian forces --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sources, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in my calculations, and I explained the reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you didn't use the testimony of Mr. Acimovic who has testified in this case received a telegram from the Zvornik Brigade command, argued with the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade about putting together an execution squad to kill the prisoners at the Rocevic school, who testified that he confronted or was confronted by Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic at the school, and that Colonel Popovic requested that a truck be brought to the school to transport the prisoners to the execution site. I take it you haven't reviewed the testimony of a witness who testified in this case who was at the site shooting at the prisoners. You don't have any familiarity with any of that, right, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, 20 or 30 minutes ago I told you that I am not familiar with a single testimony of the witnesses called by you to testify in this case, and I didn't have an opportunity to review them. Therefore, I really don't see any point in you pursuing the matter further because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, how do you know that General Smith said in his evidence that photographs were a good tool but they didn't show what was going on under the surface of the ground? How do you know that this was his evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read that in his statement. As far as I can remember, the statement can be found in the portion when Mr. Bretton Randall was putting questions to him about mass graves and said that there were photographs about those sites, and if I remember correctly, that was his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mean his statement given to the OTP, the Prosecutor's Office, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Mr. President, whether Bretton Randall was a member of the OTP or the Tribunal, what his actual role was. But if I remember correctly, it's contained in Mr. Randal's report on his interview with General Smith, and I clearly remember seeing this in this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said at page 18855 of your transcript -- I mean, of your testimony, you said that there were two ways to get out of an encirclement. One way was through a breakthrough, which was risky, and the other way was to surrender and survive. Do you remember saying that, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P2789.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we'll need to go to page 7 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a photograph -- or, rather, a still taken from video footage at Potocari, 13 July 1995. I want to direct your attention to the man on the left. His name is Mesa Efendic. He was identified by his wife as a 63-year-old man back when this video footage was taken. First of all, have you seen this particular image before? I take it no, but.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P1363. This is Mesa Efendic as he appeared in Kozluk when his remains were exhumed. You can see he's still wearing the red sweater, a light-coloured top, the dark pants. His identity was confirmed forensically in addition to this exhumation, photograph, autopsy report, everything. Do you really have much doubt that there were mass executions of Muslim prisoners that took place in the days following the collapse of Srebrenica? Is that really a question in your mind, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have any personal views, and if you remember, I answered one of your questions in the previous days of this trial to the effect that I don't claim anything. All I did was to make the calculations based on the information available to me. Likewise, I can confirm, again, to you -- and it was never my intention to claim that there were no executions and shootings because I never set that as an objective. My analysis has only shown that these executions cannot be expressed in thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you saw the picture of this man in Potocari, is there any militarily justifiable reason that I should be looking at a photograph of him now - and you, also - in an exhumation photo from the Kozluk mass grave?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, not a single killing - and I repeat - not a single killing of a disarmed member of the enemy forces is necessary and permissible. And I don't justify such acts. In my reports I never said any word to the effect that I justified any sort of killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P2530. Have you seen this document before, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, it's a document, as you can see from the heading, from the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade, from the security affairs organ, it says, to the Drina Corps command, intelligence department. And it's a report. In the report it says that on -- it's not clear what the date is, but it says: [As read] "At about 1600 hours in the general area of Buljim, the following person got away from a group heading away from Srebrenica and surrendered to the VRS." "Ibis Malic," was his name, "son of Maso, a prisoner of war, born on 1 January 1977, in the village of Sebiocina, Vlasenica municipal assembly, completed primary school, a Muslim, a member of the BH Army 281st Light East Bosnia Brigade, under the command of Mujo Hasanovic ..." Have you heard about this particular prisoner before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that the remains of Ibis Malic, born 1 January 1977, son of Maso, was recovered from Cancari 11, one of the graves that I showed you earlier?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't surprise me, sir, that he lost his life. I've just told you why this wouldn't surprise me. But let me repeat: This wouldn't surprise me because I am not claiming that there were no executions in Srebrenica during and after Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, his remains were recovered up near Zvornik. You know that. But let me ask you this: Is there any militarily justifiable reason why this barely 18-year-old young man, in the custody of VRS security organs, who was noticed to the Drina Corps command for intelligence, should be showing up coming out of a mass grave, secondary grave at that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a minute ago that there is no justification whatsoever to execute a captured and disarmed soldier from the enemy army. And a disarmed soldier from the enemy army does not pose any danger any longer due to the fact that he was disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the Court and also for your benefit, Mr. Skrbic, Mr. Malic's remains found at Cancari 11 is a secondary grave to the Branjevo farm executions that Drazen Erdemovic testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, you can find that at P167. It's e-court page 188, item number 15. Mr. President, I see it's time for our break. I think now is as good a time as any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much. We must have our first break now and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, before I forget, just as a procedural matter with respect to the next witness, my understanding is that the Prosecution should be able to achieve its cross-examination and finish its cross-examination within an hour and a half. This is based upon information that Mr. Elderkin, who has the next witness, has related to us after having spoken to Mr. Gajic. It will obviously depend, to some extent, on what's actually elicited on the stand. But he believes that he will be able to do it within that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We appreciate that, although there has not been a strict rule on that, but we know from the Prosecution case it was always with viva voce witnesses a kind of balance in relation to the time requested. Thank you very much for that. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you may recall, I believe it was on Thursday, you were asked some questions regarding a publication in which a review of your book appeared. I think you said that the publication's name was "Grom." I would like to show you 65 ter 7618.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would need to add this to the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Tolimir has, as usually, no objection. Leave is granted to add it to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you may recall that in response to a question put to you by His Honour Judge Mindua about the publication in which the review of your article appeared, you mentioned that it was an unimportant publication in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I ever said that this was not important. However, if you are asking me now, I can say that this was not one of the leading magazines or publications in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you page 2 of this magazine. We were able to find this in the library in Belgrade. And I think we have a partial translation at least of what's on the screen in front of us. But, do you recognise this, Mr. Skrbic? Is this the publication and review of your book that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have the respective page in English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think we have now in front of us the -- the headline, so to speak, and the -- what's written in the black part of this article. You do recognise it as the piece you were referring to, correct, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And it refers, once again, to the numbers that are contained in your report of 35.632 registered refugees as well as the 10- to 15.000 men who went through the breakthrough and so on. All of this is contained not only in your book but in the report that you prepared in relation to this case, yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page. That's your photograph, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you provided that for the purposes of this article, or is this something that they obtained elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they took my photo. They asked my permission, and I said go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Then we can see some documents to the right side of the screen. Are those documents you provided to the publication for the purposes of this article?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I can remember, those documents, as they are shown here, were not published in this publication. At first glance, I can say that the documents were attached to my book. They were enclosed with the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am not sure exactly what you mean by that. This is a photocopy of the publication as it appeared at the time. So when you say the documents weren't published in this publication, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the document, then I will be able to tell you whether it was used in the book and I will be able to answer your question more precisely. I need some time to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, it's not that important. The number is there. We can see it for the record, 01854496. That's one of them. And that's an ERN number. And if we go down we can see the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, perhaps that was a misunderstanding. You were asked if these documents were be -- published in this newspaper at that point in time. The question was not if they were published in your book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered that question. I said that I do not remember whether these documents were published in the publication. However, if we start from the assumption that they were, I am sure that I was not the source because the first document that I was looking at is not contained in the book. In other words, I was not the one who was able to provide that document to the publication publishers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I have my answer. Did you read this article when it was published, Mr. Skrbic, about your book?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it you don't remember seeing these documents to the right of your photograph in this publication when you read it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe it or not, as you wish, I don't remember that these documents were then published in this particular publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This particular publication, "Grom," is a weekly magazine. It's a type of tabloid, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this particular edition we can see that it's dated --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We will have to blow it up very much so that the witness can see it, but under the title "Grom" you can see very small writing. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see there the date of 26 February 2009. It's the issue number 20, Thursday edition, 30 dinars. And then I can see it says, "1 KM 0.7 euros," and so on. Your book would have to have been completed before this publication, fair to say? Early 2009 at the latest.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct. At that time I only had the manuscript. As for -- the official publication that could have been used in the way that it was used in here was the article that I submitted to the Russian academy for a conference that was supposed to take place two months later in April. So this was just the manuscript of my book. The book was finally published in March 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a clarification for Mr. Vanderpuye. Is the date 16th February or 26th February.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry about that. It's 26th February. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So this is an article based on your manuscript.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That article was used as the basis for the manuscript of my book and later for the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you had completed or at least undertaken substantially the research which is the subject matter of your expert report which you completed in 2011 as early as the beginning of 2009?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I didn't know that I would be invited as an expert in this case, so I really can't put a link between my article that I presented in Moscow and this case. The only thing being that it was used -- used as the basis for the writing of my book, and then one part of the book was used as the basis for the compilation of this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go down the page -- rather, on the second page, if we could go to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something about what's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are asking for the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, please, the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is take a look at those two pages at the bottom one by one, and maybe you can tell us what those are, Mr. Skrbic. We'll have to do them one by one so we can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just blow up the one page on the left and then we'll do the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from Mr. Robert Franken's statement. He was an OTP witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He was an OTP witness. So that's one statement that you reviewed, I guess, in relation to your manuscript, let's say. Yeah?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And later it was used in the book, this statement, and another statement provided by the same gentleman is also related to this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just take a look at the next page so that we can just identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a part of the report by General Delic sent to his Supreme Commander regarding everything that he had done for Srebrenica, i.e., for the 28th Division. Inter alia, in his report, he also says how he supplied the 28th Division and what was supplied to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Both of these are documents that appear in your book, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you were approached -- or, rather, were you approached about the possibility of this particular review of your manuscript? Or is this something you solicited?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was not my request. A journalist approached me. He asked me whether I was prepared to give a statement for his newspaper and I said yes. I said I was ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it you provided him with a copy of your manuscript, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you're aware that this was going to be published in a -- I would imagine a reasonably circulated publication?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I showed him the manuscript in support of my statement. I didn't know that he would be using enclosures to my manuscript because those enclosures were nothing but corroborating evidence to the manuscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Enclosures aside, you knew that this publication was going to circulate a review of your article in which you claim, in effect, that Srebrenica didn't happen, that the casualties that had been proven time and time again following the fall of Srebrenica to Muslim prisoners never happened. Right, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, never, ever did I say that Srebrenica did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say that 397 people are potential victims of the collapse of Srebrenica and died most probably inappropriately at the hands of Serb forces, with all due respect, Mr. Skrbic, you are saying that Srebrenica never happened. Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You cannot ascribe that to me. At the very beginning of my testimony, I said that I didn't claim that crimes never happened, that executions never happened. I never claimed that. Sir, if you have read my book carefully, you could see that somewhere in the introduction to that book I say that my mother is not sadder than a Muslim mother, that my mother doesn't cry more pitifully than a Muslim mother, and I really believe that. I truly believe that. Please do not ascribe to me what I never said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you tell General Tolimir that you had published a paper and written a book about the subject matter of your report in this case?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I have told you that the first time I met General Tolimir here in this courtroom, how could I have then told him anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Gajic or anyone associated with the Defence of General Tolimir that you had written a paper and written a book in advance of preparing your report on the population of Srebrenica that you submitted in this case?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gajic knew that I had published that book and that some of the materials included in the book would make it into my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You say some of the material, Mr. Skrbic. In fact, from about page 72 to page 229 of your book - which is the last page of it - is virtually identical to your report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not sure about them being identical. I've told you that my first expert report, the one that we are discussing right now, was based on my book. I never denied that. Not for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am not just talking about it being based on your book, Mr. Skrbic - and maybe my question was imprecise - but it's virtually identical. That's a little bit different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be sure about that. I wouldn't say that they are absolutely identical. If you were to ask me about percentages, whether it's 70, 80, 90 per cent, I wouldn't be able to give you the percentage, but I am not denying that, yes, there are similarities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it's possible to do this but let me ask: Is it possible to display these two exhibits side by side, one is D368 and the other one is 65 ter 602 -- 7602. Are we able to do that in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We have your book on the left. We have your report on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 10 in the report on the right, in e-court, and page 71 in the book on the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The pages are identical. Mr. Vanderpuye asked for another one. Page 10 in the report on the right side. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just focus in on the charts, it would probably be easier for everybody to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Aside from the changes in column two, from three, four, five, and six, to B, C, D, and E, are there any substantive changes to this document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 78 in the book and page 15 in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Anything different here, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only in the manner of annotation and marking because in the book, I had to change the way I marked the colours because it was expensive for me to have the book printed in colour; therefore, I introduced those changes in order for a reader to be able to understand which number represents what. On the other hand, in the report everything is depicted in colours, and although that was my intention to do the same in my book, as I said, it was too expensive. As you may remember, I said that I was looking for a sponsor for someone to help me publish my book, and I even approached some of the political parties, but I failed in that and I had to undertake the publishing of my book on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I am going to move to a different section on this point, but just for the record, you will find similar comparisons at page 85 in e-court in the book and page 20 in the report; page 86 in e-court -- okay, we can do them, but I just -- I think it might be better to just put on the record what they are. This one I think is at page 85. Do you see that, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And they are the same, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just for the record - and we won't need to go to this - we have a similar comparison at page 86 in e-court and 21 in the report; page 91 in e-court, page 24 in the report; and page 95 in e-court, page 27 in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I want to ask you a little bit about your military analysis at this point. As I understand your report with respect to the forcible transfer of the Muslim populations of Srebrenica and Zepa, it is your position that they wanted to leave those areas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that it was their choice to leave those areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And we demonstrated that last Wednesday, if I am not wrong, in document P190 or something. But anyway, we demonstrated that to be a fact when the president of the Presidency of Srebrenica municipality asked the political authorities in Sarajevo to give him an approval for an arrangement with the Army of Republika Srpska, for him to reach an agreement with them so that the VRS would open a corridor for the population to move out. And I established that this happened long before the 9th of July, 1995. That is to say, that either identical or a similar attempt was made back in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, I put it to you that the Muslim population in Srebrenica and in Zepa in 1995 were left with no genuine choice but to leave the enclave and that was as a result of a policy that was put in place by the VRS and the civilian authorities to rid those areas of the Muslim population and other areas, frankly, in Eastern Bosnia, a policy that went back as far as 1992. What do you say?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you that I avoided as much as possible, although it was not always possible, to avoid dealing with politics because no army - neither the VRS nor any other army - is involved in politics. Everybody knows exactly how an army operates vis-a-vis politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you P2495 and then another document, and I will ask you for your comment. You can see that this is a document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's dated 19 November 1992. And it's entitled: "Directive for Further Operations of the Army of Republika Srpska," to the commander, Chief of Staff personally, directive operational number 4. Have you seen this document before, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen it in its entirety. I do know, however, that it exists and I know of Directive Number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to page number 5 in English, and I believe it's page 10 in the B/C/S. Page 11 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Under item number D -- or, rather, item labeled D, it refers to the Drina Corps. It says as follows: "The Drina Corps: From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population." Let me just clarify a couple of things with you. The Birac area includes Srebrenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Birac area includes Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I want to focus you on the area -- or, rather, the sentence here that talks about forcing the enemy to leave the area of Birac, Zepa, Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population. You understand that to be civilian population as distinguished from the army, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P2434. This is a document dated 24 November 1992. It's issued by the Drina Corps command. You will see that it's signed by -- I think it's Colonel Milenko Zivanovic at that time. And it says very urgent decision for further operations. And it's directed to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade command. And it reads at the beginning as follows: "Pursuant to the directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential number 02/5 of 19 November 1992," which is the document we just saw, "and an assessment of the situation, I have decided: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up, or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." That falls in line with the document we just saw, right, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you agree, Mr. Skrbic, that it is wholly illegal for the army to force the local Muslim population to abandon the areas of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that an army must fall -- can force the population to do anything. But, sir, immediately from the very outset of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, members of all ethnic communities always left the territory that was not under the control of their own respective army. That was the rule and that's how all the three ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina behaved, the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats. Nobody was prepared to remain in the territory controlled by the enemy army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What's the reason for putting that as an objective in this document, then, if it goes without saying, as you argue?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what were the reasons that prompted this commander to phrase it like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If those units followed this order, they would be forcing those people to leave those areas. Right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, a war is something which is unendurable and unacceptable for any population. If these units were carrying out the tasks given them by their superior officers of defeating and inflicting as many losses as possible, which I personally would never phrase like that because it implies an indefinite number, then it means that these units were engaged in combat legally and legitimately with members of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We all see the part in this decision that calls for units to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses and to exhaust them and break them up and to force them to surrender. What I am asking you specifically about is this additional task which calls for them to force the Muslim local population to abandon the areas of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. That's distinct. If those units were following that decision with respect to the movement of that population, they would be forcing that population to leave in the terms of this order; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If units of the Drina Corps were defeating the 28th Division and if the 28th Division had to be pushed back or if it had to pull out from those positions, then you are right. In that way the population would have been forced to leave the area because they wouldn't want to remain there without their own army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Why would a corps commander order his units to force out the population separately and apart from any other combat activity relating to the army?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a separate order. It goes side by side with the order to engage in combat with the 28th Division. You can see it for yourself. That's how it's written here. I already answered your question by saying that I honestly don't know why the commander put this sentence in this order in this manner. I never had an opportunity to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One reason might be that the commander wanted it carried out as he wrote it, militarily. Right, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you an answer a moment ago. If you believe that a forcible relocation of the population who is pulling out ahead of their own army, which was being defeated, in that case I accept your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P2158. This is a document from 1994, dated 4 July. It's from the Bratunac Brigade command. And it's written by Slavko Ognjenovic who was the commander of that brigade at that time. I'd like to take you to page 2 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We will need to go to the very bottom of the page in the English and the top of the page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to the first paragraph -- first full paragraph in the B/C/S. At the very bottom of the page it reads in English: "We have won the war in Podrinje, but we have not beaten the Muslims." We will need to go to the next page in English.
