"We have not beaten the Muslims completely, which is what we must do in the next period. We must attain our final goal - an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde must be defeated militarily. "We must continue to arm, train, discipline, and prepare the RS Army for the execution of this crucial task - the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave. "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave, we must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Have you seen this document before Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it accurately states what the VRS objective towards Srebrenica was, which was the expulsion of Muslims there; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but have you noticed that in the last paragraph it is said that it should be temporarily achieved. It does not necessarily mean permanently. If you haven't noticed it yet, maybe you can look at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, the translation we have - and it may be just a translation issue - but the translation says that: "The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." The temporariness in this sentence refers to how long the Muslims will be staying in the enclave, not how long they will have been gone once they are expelled, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there is no need whatsoever to construe or to comment upon anything because everything is stated here clearly. I am going to repeat it for you. "The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible." When you speak about enemy, a soldier or an officer, understand that to mean another army. Not people. And this clearly speaks about temporary stay in the enclave. So, in other words, there is no explicit order for the enclave to be abandoned permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Part of this language that refers to leaving the enclave en masse refers to an army, Mr. Skrbic? Have you ever seen language referring to an army leaving en masse?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, sir. And I have personal experience of that. The Army of Republika Srpska left western municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina such as Glamoc, Bosansko Grahovo, Drvar, Bosanski Petrovac, Kljuc, and Sanski Most en masse, including Mrkonjic Grad. Ahead of the army or alongside the army, the local population amounting to 90.000 Serbs abandoned the areas en masse as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Skrbic. Did those Serbs leave the area because they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't want to stay in the territory that was not under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska because they feared for their safety and that was the reason why they wanted to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P1214.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We will have to go to the second page in the English so that we can see what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see that it's issued under the supreme -- well, rather, by the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska. It's entitled: "Directive for Further Operations No. 7," yes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me take you to page 10 in the English and 15 in the B/C/S. You will see at the -- in the middle of the page a reference to the Drina Corps. Do you see that, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I want to direct your attention to the second sentence -- or, rather, beginning the second sentence of that paragraph, which reads: "As many enemy forces as possible should be tied down by diversionary and active combat operations on the north-west part of the war front, using operational and ... camouflage measures, while in the direction of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves. By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica or Zepa." Are you familiar with that language, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And creating a situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the Muslim inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa would make them want to leave, right, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't necessarily mean that that would make them leave because this was never explicitly ordered. It was never ordered that things should be done so as to make them leave or so as to expel them. Sir, war, i.e., armed combat, as the most important -- or the most prevalent segment of any war is an unbearable situation for any population, irrespective of whose population it is. And I am talking about the population belonging to any of the two warring parties. It is not necessary to create additionally worse situation because war is bad enough. War already creates an unbearable situation. So the situation started being unbearable when war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the situation was equally unbearable for all the three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a directive signed by the president - right? - Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It was prepared with the input, consideration and advice of the Main Staff of the VRS, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to standard military procedures, that should be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, we can go to the last page of this document in the -- I think in both languages, or it's the next-to-last page in English, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's the next-to-last page in the B/C/S, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you go down to the bottom of the page you can see that it was drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic, the same Miletic in whose Defence you were employed as an investigator; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And he was a member of the Main Staff at the time that this directive was drafted; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, too, is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the language that relates to imposing upon the inhabitants of Srebrenica conditions where they have no hope of further survival or life is somehow superfluous language? Because that just goes without saying because it's war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. I said that war, i.e., armed combat, as the most important of segment of war, is already unbearable enough for any population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, if we can go to page 21 in the B/C/S - we might already be there - and page 14 in the English, I'd like to ask you about this. You will see a reference here where it -- the sentence begins: "The relevant state and military organs ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are we able to locate that in the B/C/S? I believe it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You should be able to see [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can this be shown to me? Can your assistant show it to me? I am still on the last page is what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I am referring to should actually be on the next page. It's under item 6.1. It's the third paragraph. So it should be at the top of the next page in the B/C/S. It's the second full paragraph on that page. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if this is the paragraph started with the words "via authorised state and military bodies ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. It says: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our good will, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Have you seen this before, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already told you that I saw the entire directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you know that this isn't just a matter of making war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, war is not only armed combat. War encompasses a series of other segments. I don't want to go into all of them, but they would start with media and propaganda activities, material activities, diplomatic activities, and let me stop here. War encompasses all of that. And I said that armed conflict is its most important or extreme segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You still maintain that the Srebrenica and Zepa populations left those areas voluntarily, of their own free choice; is that right, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I still adhere by the position that the Muslim population voluntarily and of their own accord abandoned the area. They simply didn't want to stay behind in a territory that had been abandoned by the 28th Division when they faced the activities of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And making their life unbearable with no hope of survival or life had nothing to do with it. Is that your position, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, everything that happened in July 1995, everything that was caused by the 28th Division, all combat activities that were carried out by the 28th Division against the Drina Corps compounded the situation and the life of the population of Srebrenica in Srebrenica itself. How was their life compounded by that? The Drina Corps and the other units of the Army of Republika Srpska had to and had the legitimate right to respond to any combat activities launched by the 28th Division against the former units, and this is how the unbearable situation was further compounded. Particularly in view of the fact that we are also talking about fire being opened in urban areas where combatants and civilian population are intermixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask one question. Sorry for interrupting you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I understand your position that these unbearable situations are a logical consequence of war. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why is it then necessary to write that down in a directive or an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've already answered that. I said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, you didn't answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I don't know why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why that was written in the directive and in the previous document that was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It was your understanding -- or maybe you correct me if I am wrong, is it your understanding that it was the intention that the Muslim population leave those areas on a temporary basis? Is that what you've argued in your report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was your understanding that their removal from the enclaves was to be permanent?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not conclude that they were removed from the enclave. I concluded based on the documents that I presented in my report that they left the enclave of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P241. While that's coming up, let me tell you this is a MUP intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It shouldn't be broadcast. I'm sorry, Mr. President. I understand that we can broadcast it, so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think so, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's dated 12 July, 1995. The time is 1250. And this is an intercept of a conversation involving General Mladic, relative to the removal of the civilian population from Srebrenica. X says: "Go ahead, General." Mladic says: "Have these buses and trucks left?" X: "They have." Mladic: "When?" X: "Ten minutes ago." Mladic says: "Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They have all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all. Those who want to and those who don't want to." X says: "I understand, general." Mladic says: "Don't issue any statements and don't interrupt them over the radio station. We will open a corridor towards Kladanj." Mladic says: "Indeed. Let it pass there. Take a patrol of ours to wait on the road and remove the mines and obstacles." It's unheard what's said. And then it says: "Leave the territory." X replies: "Yes, general." Those who want to and those who don't want to, Mr. Skrbic. Do you see a choice in there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that. However, I do see where it says that those who want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. I want to show you P94 once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we'll need to go to page 266. That would be 268.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a photograph, as you can see, a composite of the mosque standing in Srebrenica. First of all, have you seen this photograph before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you the next page, please. This is what it looked like after Srebrenica fell. Have you seen this photograph, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this photograph before. However, I have seen plenty of such scenes during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P2178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can it be turned around?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can probably tell this is an aerial image of Zepa, 27 July 1995. And let me show you the next page of this document. This is aerial imagery taken of the same area on the 24th of August, and what we have that you can see in all of these boxes are destroyed buildings since the 27th of July, 1995. Have you seen this image before? And separately from that, are you aware that there was widespread destruction of these buildings following the expulsion of the Muslim population in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this photograph before. I believe you when you say that there were a lot of damaged buildings, buildings that were destroyed, but I can't confirm for a fact that it really happened when you say because I've already presented my position vis-a-vis photos. During combat in urban areas, buildings have to be destroyed, particularly those buildings from which defendants tend to open fire on the attackers. That happens. And that kind of situation is more complicated than combat which takes place in other environments. In theory there is a reference to one special kind of operation and that operation takes place in urban areas and those operations are different than operations in any other circumstances. I believe you that buildings were destroyed during the war in settled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Like I said, this is a photograph of the buildings that were destroyed since July 27th, 1995. Let me show you another set of photographs at pages 5 and 6. We'll start with 5. This is a photograph -- or, rather, an aerial image of the mosque, the central mosque in Zepa, 27th of July, 1995. Can you see that on your screen or do we need to make it bigger for you to see?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's blow that up, if we can, so that he can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me take you to page 6 and we will take a look at the same image. This again shows the buildings that were destroyed in that area since July 27th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we can focus in on the middle, we'll be able to take a look at the central mosque at that time. Can you blow it up a little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see anything in there, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the ruins.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said you were aware of this kind of thing happening throughout the war. In this particular case, in Srebrenica and Zepa, I have now shown you pictures of destroyed mosques. Do you have any explanation for that? Can you tell us what is the military impetus behind destroying a religious building such as a mosque? What's the military value of that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a facility is not used as a military stronghold, either as a fire nest or a protection facility, such a facility cannot be a military target. However, if a facility is used as protection or it -- which provides military advantage or if it's used to open fire from it, then such a facility is a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who would have been using that facility in Zepa after the 27th of July, 1995, to carry out combat operations if nobody was there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were no troops. I have already answered that such a facility cannot be a legitimate military target and that such a facility should not be destroyed. I repeat: In my expert report, I did not claim that there were no crimes comitted in Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll leave it there, Mr. Skrbic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are -- we will have soon our break. I think it's better to have our break before you commence your re-examination, Mr. Tolimir. I will put one final question to the witness. Sir, we dealt a lot with your book and the publication in the newspaper. Only one question. The title of the book is: "Genocide of the Truth," or "... Against the Truth," or I have read some other translations. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the full title of the book is: "Srebrenica, Genocide Comitted Against the Truth." What I meant by that was that genocide was comitted against truth, the truth about all the events surrounding Srebrenica, and that I based on the results of the analysis that I carried out. What I meant was that truth was destroyed and that is not good, either for the Serbs or the Muslims. The best thing for all would be to accept the truth because only the truth can lead to the reconciliation of the peoples and only in that way a normal life would continue in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your view, sir, who comitted this kind of genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, that genocide was comitted by the Muslim side. The extreme elements of the Muslim policy and politics in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am specifically referring to the title, "Genocide of Truth," or "... Committed Against the Truth." Who comitted genocide against the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just answered. The official politics in Sarajevo. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have our second break now and we will resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we continue with the testimony of the witness, Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, is the next witness already here in the Tribunal and is he waiting? Mr. Gajic? Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. I am receiving French translation on the channel that is reserved for the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I repeat my question: Is the next witness already here in the Tribunal and is he waiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Then we can call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you what do you expect -- how many time you will need for the re-examination, Mr. Tolimir? If it will take some time of the last session, we should release the witness. What is your estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am of the opinion that we should release the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should do that and he will then be called tomorrow afternoon. Now we continue with the examination of Mr. Skrbic. Judge Mindua has a question, first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, indeed, I would like to go back very briefly to the operation that the 28th Division was supposed to carry out, the breakthrough operation that the 28th Division of the ABiH was to carry. So I would like to -- you to tell us, as a military expert, what happens in a case such as the one of the 28th Division? What was the objective of the breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last part was not heard in the English channel. I received the French original, but if is there is nothing missing ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the goal? Why did the 28th Division carry out the breakthrough? And I am talking about the 28th Division of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every unit that either intentionally or unintentionally remains in encirclement has one sole objective and that is to make a breakthrough in as compact form as possible, to have a rest after the breakthrough, to be remanned, and to prepare itself for the following combat operations. This is a universal rule applicable to all armies. The objective of the breakthrough of the 28th Division was exactly as I described; that is to say, to breakthrough, to have a rest, to increase the number of staff to the required level, to become equipped, and to be able to carry out further tasks received from their superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I thought that the goal of the breakthrough was to enable the 28th Division to get out of the encirclement and to reach the territory of the ABiH. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. You understood well. A breakthrough is always carried out in the direction of the closest unit that can provide support during the breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Then in a similar case, could we think that a commander would leave an opening so as to enable the enemy troops to leave the territory which was under his control? And I will try to be a bit more precise. The VRS, could they let the 28th Division go through so that it reaches the territory of the ABiH? Was that possible? Is that a scenario that could have been possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was possible. And then we have the following situation: If the commander of the unit across whose zone the breakthrough is being carried out makes an assessment that if he tightens the ring and does everything possible to prevent the breakthrough, then under such a scenario he would incur considerable losses. Then, for the benefit of the safety of his own men, makes it incumbent on such a commander to open up a corridor or a route along which the enemy can pull out while, at the same time, he will prevent his own men from being killed during the breakthrough. There are quite a few examples of that nature in history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And you are very right, in fact. We heard a witness of the VRS who also corroborated this. But tell me this: When a breakthrough is carried out, according to the military doctrine, is it necessary to respect a sort of proportionality when it comes to the people who are controlling the territory? And I will be a little bit more precise. You said that the VRS, which was opposing to the breakthrough of the 28th Division, had used all the means that they had at their disposal, all the artillery weaponry, explosives, mines, et cetera, et cetera, in such a way that the BiH soldiers experienced great losses. We have heard here a commander of the VRS who said that he wanted to put an end to the use of some weapons in order to avoid huge losses of BiH members, who were falling like flies. So this is my question: Does the military doctrine, as taught in academies, teach you to reduce the fire-power in order to create too many victims and not to cause too much damage when it comes to the opposite army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main factors that determine the level of the use of force in an armed conflict is, first and foremost, the requirements of the tasks given by -- to the subordinate command. The second one is the safety of the troops carrying it out. Anyway, I would like to say that an excessive use of force does not exist as a phrase in military doctrine. There is another definition which says that force should be used as little as possible, and the best way of carrying out a task is not to consume too many assets, and the best way is to defeat an enemy without fighting at all, as rightly put 200 years ago by a great Chinese thinker, Sun Tzu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. I would now like to ask you something about your methodology. When it came to the population of Srebrenica, how did you establish some facts. You stated that you were not necessarily interested in exhumations, and you did not focus on other evidence. What you really wanted to see is that -- is how many people lived in Srebrenica before the events in July and you wanted to establish what was the population number after the July events. So this is my first question to you: Before July you are talking about the population which lived in Srebrenica, but when you talk about the period before July and before the events, what dates do you have in mind? And I would like to compare that figure with the figure which exists for the period following the month of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The initial information that I presented in my expert report and which I showed in table 1 was January 1994. The next piece of information relates to the situation in January 1995, and finally, I had information that pertained to July 1995. So these are the numbers of inhabitants that I used in my calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So at that point, we have to think about the population which lives in Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So now tell us this: After the events, the total number of survivors, according to you, where are they? Are they now still in Srebrenica or are they elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The survivors that I describe as refugees from Srebrenica were from the Srebrenica enclave, which means not only the town proper of Srebrenica but Srebrenica enclave or from the area described by the term "safe haven."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And I hope that this is my last question. I am quite confused because we have different figures. If we take into account the exhumation, we get two different figures, because you make a difference between the population before and after. So I would like to know the following: Did you take into account in your evaluation of the population after, so the survivors, in your calculations, did you take into account that amongst those survivors there were some people who were not taken into account in January and in July and who may have come from somewhere else - we don't know from where - and that are now amongst your survivors, and maybe those survivors are, in fact, mainly refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may have been refugees, but in the document that I used from the scheme or the graph given in the briefing, it is clearly said that 35.632 were refugees from Srebrenica, the refugees from the Srebrenica enclave, and this is the figure that I relied upon in my calculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tolimir, it's your turn to commence your re-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Greetings to the witness, and I wish him a pleasant stay amongst us. And I would like to have this day in court finalised according to God's will and not my wishes. Mr. Skrbic, Judge Mindua asked you about the breakthrough. Let us summarise this in one question which is: If the 28th Division initiated a breakthrough and took with them all the people who were capable of work, and all the women, children, and the elderly sent -- were sent to the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir please repeat the last part of his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the last part of your question was not interpreted to us. The sentence stopped when you said: "... all these people were sent to the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari ..." And after that we didn't hear anything. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Women, children, and the elderly were sent to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. By such conduct of the authorities who took this decision, did it mean that it was decided that the Srebrenica enclave is to be abandoned?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to separate the population of Srebrenica or, rather, to divide them into two groups, or -- one group was made up of women, children, and the elderly, and the second group was made up of members of the 28th Division including other able-bodied men, and I find this division to be quite interested [as interpreted] and it merits additional research in order to arrive at a relevant conclusion. I wonder, how is it possible that those who must be most concerned about their families, how is it possible that they send their families to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari which, to all intents and purposes, amounts to abandonment, and then they decided that they themselves would launch a breakthrough. The only reasonable conclusion that I myself can arrive at would be the following. The Muslims of Srebrenica, including their civilian local authorities and the command of the 28th Division, were convinced that the population would be relocated to Tuzla and its environs and that the Serbian forces would not harm them. Otherwise, why would they leave their families? It doesn't make sense. Why would they leave all the women, children, and the elderly in the territory that was nearly under the control of the VRS? Although, they didn't yet have their units in the territory, they might have exert this control by fire alone. Now, the only reasonable conclusion as I see it is that they expected the population to be relocated to Tuzla, and that once they carry out the breakthrough, they would reunite with their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. I am on my feet for two reasons. The first is, obviously, in relation to the speculative answer that was given by the witness who first said that he would have to undertake additional study in order to provide a reasoned response, and then proceeded to provide a response. The second has to do with the nature and the scope of the questions that General Tolimir intends to put to the witness. Since he is on redirect examination, I would ask that he put questions that arise from the cross-examination of this witness. The question of abandoning -- or abandoning the enclave by sending women and children to Potocari was not broached at all during the cross-examination. It is the subject of the witness's report but he wasn't cross-examined on it. So to the extent that he intends put questions in redirect, I would ask that he at least lay a reasonable foundation in order to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do have a comment. My question was based on the four or five questions that were posed by Judge Mindua. I now want to ask another question based on a number of questions put to the witness by Mr. Vanderpuye about bearable and unbearable conditions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you will remember that the Prosecutor asked you several questions about unbearable conditions. My question is this: If Srebrenica and Zepa were declared demilitarised zones in the territory of Republika Srpska and, thus, they became enclaves, and they did not accept the status of demilitarised zones but, rather, launched attacks on the civilians and the troops of the VRS - it was the VRS that gave those zones the status of demilitarised zones - did they have the right to remove that status from them, given the fact that they were not demilitarised? What does the international law say about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica enclave did not receive the status as a demilitarised zone. By a Security Council resolution, it was declared a protected area by the United Nations. Based on an agreement and bearing in mind the text of the Security Council resolution, it should have also become a demilitarised zone. In case the Muslim side did not comply with that agreement and it did not allow for demilitarisation to be carried out under the control and supervision of the United Nations, would -- then any attack against the units of the 28th Division, according to the criteria of UN Protection Forces, could not satisfy the standards of definition of attacks against the demilitarised zone. This was confirmed by the UNPROFOR commander and you can find that, as far as I can remember, in paragraph 45 of the Secretary-General's report. However, I am not absolutely sure that it was, indeed, paragraph 45, but I am sure that in the UN Secretary-General's report you will find that the position of the UNPROFOR commander was exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up P2873, page 2. Thank you. While we are waiting, I would like to put my question to the witness. And the document can be used to lay the foundation for my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye asked you about the number that you took as the basis for your calculations. Please, I don't want to repeat things. You just simply tell us this: Did any authorities or international organisations refute the information about the number of refugees and militarily able-bodied men who arrived in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if we could have the B/C/S version of that on the screen. Although, it might be a problem because this is the Prosecution document, but earlier we have seen I think a Defence document with this -- to that was the B/C/S translation attached. Can you help us, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then go ahead, please, Mr. Tolimir. Thank you, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is this: If the government in Sarajevo and the International Red Cross on the 4th of August, 1995, published this information for the general public and for their respective institutions, did any institution, did any organisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina challenge or refute the information about those who abandoned Srebrenica and arrived in the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard, nor did I come across a document in which you can see that anybody on any side refuted this information and that's why I use that as a -- the stable basis and the stable fact that I used in my calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: The survivors, as an indicator, would there be a more reliable piece of evidence than the lists of those who went missing when it comes to using the methodology of research that is based on survivors as opposed to those who died or were killed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obviously believe that the methodology that I used in my research is reliable and even more reliable than the methodology which implies looking for victims. It's very difficult to research victims. It is much easier to follow the movement of the surviving population and in that way establish any possible differences. However, it was not up to me to provide the final evaluation. The final evaluation is in the hands of the Trial Chamber and the Honourable Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up P1777, P1777. This is a list provided by the OTP in 2009. This is a list of those who went missing and even the locations where they were buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't mention the names. Don't mention the real name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at D316. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the same name, the name that was under number 7 (redacted) (redacted) Now we can see a decision for that same person or in respect of that same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are still waiting for the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D316. I would kindly ask the e-court to display D316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is always helpful to give us the correct number in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat the number: D316. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Now we can see a decision or a ruling about the establishment of the death of that individual who was under number 7. It says in the first paragraph that he was killed on the 7th of July, 1995. And there is also an indication of the place where he was killed and that was a street called Ljubisavici. And in the following paragraph it says that the witnesses who were present during his execution confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this specific circumstance, this should not be broadcast, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shouldn't be broadcast, and I don't want to read it, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But look at the second paragraph, the fourth line from the top, you will see that he was buried in a graveyard known as Kazan. My question is this: If you have managed to link the information that I have just presented, would you say that the entry under number 7 in the OTP's list from 2009 that we saw as Exhibit P1777 differs from what we see on the screen now? Would you say that the two sets of information provided about that same individual differ from one document to the next? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The two sets of information are completely different. There is no doubt about that when we look at the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If he were to appear on the list of survivors, or if he were to be identified as a survivor, would you say that that would be an even more reliable proof than any of the lists of missing people?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he -- if a census were to be carried out and if that person were to be found on the census, that would certainly be the most reliable proof that he is still living. The second relevant proof, the second most important proof, would be the register of deceased or deaths because that register contains all the names of the individuals who died either of natural causes or who suffered the forcible death in peacetime or a forcible death in a war or if they were simply killed during the war. In any case, such an individual is registered in the register of death, and then that list from the register of death, in my opinion, would be a very important source of information about the missing, those who were killed, those who died, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Let us look at the second paragraph, the second line from the top, and you will see that the command of the 28th Division, on the 19th of March, 1997, issued a certificate where it says that this person - whose name I am not going to mention - got killed on the elevation Ljubisavici near Srebrenica which means -- this is my question: (redacted)
